Let's see what happens when we use less aggressive augmentations.  As some reasonable inter-class confusion could be happening due to lighting changes causing a kernel to appear healthy/defective, cropping removing the kernel damage, etc.

learn = train(arch, item=Resize((256,256),
    method=ResizeMethod.Pad, pad_mode=PadMode.Zeros),
    batch=aug_transforms(size=(256,256), min_scale=1,
        max_zoom=0.0, max_lighting=0.0, p_lighting=0.0,
        max_warp=0.0, p_affine=0.0))

These results seem to indicate that simply decreasing the augmentation transforms to this degree will encourage overfitting even faster.  Might need to find a balance between the degree/type of augmentations for the larger networks.

evidence_occurrences.evidence_text:
Labeled images were split into training (0.9) and validation (0.1) sets in a stratified manner resulting in 71423 training examples and 8010 validation examples belonging to 1584 classes.

The model I've built assumes fixed-size inputs, so the first preprocessing step was to resize each image's smallest dimension to 256 pixels (retaining the aspect ratio) and then cropping it at the center of the larger dimension, obtaining 256x256 images. Some information gets lost during this process and an alternative approach where multiple crops are taken from the same image was considered, but not used for the final solution due to much longer training times (bigger, but more correlated training set). Furthermore, mean values were subtracted from each feature in the data and the obtained values were normalized by dividing each dimension by its standard deviation. Preprocessing data statistics were computed from the subset of training instances. During the training phase random transformations (rotations, zooms, shifts, shears and flips) were applied to data in order to reduce overfitting. The latter assures that our model only rarely sees exactly the same example more than once. For exact transformation parameters see [data_provider.py](painters/data_provider.py#L41).

evidence_occurrences.evidence_text:
*   Adapting the normalization layer with the global mean and deviation of the 2020 Cassava dataset
*   5-fold-CV with 20 epochs with early stopping and callback for restoring weights of best epoch
*   Final model was trained for 14 epochs on whole competition data set
*   For inference we used simple test time augmentations (Flip, Rotate, Transpose). To do so, we cropped 4 overlapping patches of size 512x512px from the .jpg images (800x600px) and applied 2 augmentations to each patch. We retained two additional center-cropped patches of the image to which no augmentations were applied. To get an overall prediction, we took the average of all these image tiles.

Finally, our ensemble included a pretrained **CropNet (MobileNetv3)** Model from Tensorflow Hub:

*   We used a pretrained model from TensorFlow Hub called [CropNet](https://tfhub.dev/google/cropnet/classifier/cassava_disease_V1/2) which was specifically trained to detect Cassava leaf diseases
*   The CropNet model is based on the MobileNetV3 architecture. We decided not to do any additional fine-tuning of that model.
*   As stated in the description the images must be rescaled to 224x224 pixel which is pretty small. We achieved good results by not just resizing our 512x512 training images but to center crop them first.
*   As the notebooks had to be submitted without internet access, it was necessary to cache the model before including it. You can find more information on this on the official [TF Hub website](https://www.tensorflow.org/hub/caching) or alternatively in this post on [Medium](https://xianbao-qian.medium.com/how-to-run-tf-hub-locally-without-internet-connection-4506b850a915).

lessons.title: Randomize valid molecular strings for training and median TTA
lessons.statement: When a molecular text model is sensitive to equivalent string serialization, consider this source-backed action: Generate chemically equivalent randomized SMILES and compare training augmentation and median TTA separately. evidence_occurrences.evidence_text:
2.   **Finetuning:** Most aspects of this were very standard for a BERT finetuning script - AdamW optimizer, no layers frozen, one cycle learning rate schedule with linear annealing, automatic mixed precision, learning rate + batch size + epoch count tuned using optuna, gradient norms clipped to 1, etc. The only things that felt a bit unusual or domain-specific were the data augmentation strategy and use of separate learning rate schedules (with different max_lr values) for the regression head and the backbone. Data augmentation is discussed more in its own section later. As for the dual max_lr trick (to set the head's learning rate to a value higher than the one used for the backbone), I heard of people doing that before, and had heard it is commonly beneficial for small datasets, but had never used it myself. For most foundation models and target properties in this competition, I found it slightly beneficial to set the head learning rates an order of magnitude higher than the backbone learning rates. The training datasets were relatively small, so that wasn't too surprising.

**Data augmentation:**

*   **Training-time augmentation:** During both pretraining and finetuning, I used `Chem.MolToSmiles(..., canonical=False, doRandom=True, isomericSmiles=True)` to create 10 non-canonical SMILES per input SMILES to increase the amount of training data ~10x. I also tried randomly using Kukulized SMILES, removing stereochemistry, and making the hydrogens & bonds more explicit, but those augmentations were not beneficial.
*   **Test-time augmentation:** My inference code generates 50 predictions per SMILE using the same data augmentation strategy used during training, just with the amount of random variation increased 5x. The final predictions for each BERT model were the median of those 50 predictions.

Test time augmentation alone provided a LB improvement of ~0.01 in one early experiment. My notes are too badly fragmented to say exactly how much the training data augmentation helped without additional ablation testing, but I'm under the impression it was very beneficial too, and a training data augmentation factor of 10x was optimal to within a margin of +/- 30% (unlike test time augmentation, more is not better).
